description:
🌎 We are a passionate team from Bolivia participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026!

We are a group of curious, creative, and motivated people interested in technology, science, innovation, and solving real-world problems. We enjoy learning, sharing ideas, and turning challenges into meaningful solutions.

For this challenge, we are excited to explore NASA's Earth observation data, investigate environmental changes, and make science more accessible through technology.

Why join our team?

We believe great ideas come from collaboration, diverse perspectives, and teamwork. We offer a supportive environment where everyone can contribute, learn, experiment, and grow together.

Skills we are looking for:

Data analysis and visualization.

Web development and programming.

UI/UX design and creativity.

Earth science, climate, or environmental knowledge.

Research, storytelling, and presentation skills.

If you are curious, passionate about innovation, and ready to make an impact, we would love to have you on our team! 🚀
summary:
APU is a web learning app that turns students into Earth system trend detectives. It teaches them to answer a real question with real NASA data: is the snow on our mountains actually disappearing, or does it only seem so?

APU follows Dr. James Aker’s five-step method: variable, region, period, time series and significance. Students learn the method in 10 lessons, then apply it in 11 real mountain-range cases. In each case they explore NASA data on a 3D mountain, run the same statistics scientists use (Mann-Kendall, Sen’s slope and the Hamed-Rao correction) and sign their own verdict. The data includes MODIS snow cover, GPM IMERG precipitation, GRACE ice mass and GLIMS glacier outlines.

The main case is Bolivia’s Cordillera Real. In the dry season, up to 27% of La Paz’s water comes from meltwater. The city faced water rationing in 2016 and a red alert in August 2026. In APU, students discover for themselves that the range’s dry-season snow cover is declining (p = 0.008). They also learn to say “we don’t know” when the data isn’t conclusive.

APU doesn’t solve the water crisis. It prepares the generation that will face it.
details:
What it does and how it works
APU is a web learning app that teaches students to investigate, with real NASA data, whether mountain snow and glaciers are changing. The name means “sacred mountain” in Quechua and Aymara. Students follow Dr. James Aker’s five-step method: variable → region → period → time series → significance (“real or luck?”).

The experience has two stages:

  1. Learning path: 10 lessons in three blocks.
    • Variables: what satellites observe; rainfall that feeds the mountains.
    • Tools: MODIS, Terra and Aqua; how MODIS detects snow (NDSI, thresholds, quality flags).
    • Method: building a hypothesis, choosing a region and period, cleaning data, testing significance, and judging the verdict, including El Niño and the method’s limits.
  2. Detective cases: 11 case files, one per mountain range: Bolivia’s Cordillera Real, Cordillera Blanca, Himalaya, Alps, Alaska, Karakoram, Greenland, Kilimanjaro, Patagonia, Vatnajökull and Antarctica. Each case follows seven clues: File → Evidence → Scene → Time → Tracks → Interrogation → Verdict.

In the Tracks clue, students play the time series in sync with a 3D mountain. In Interrogation they see the trend, the p-value and a five-check traffic light. They finish by signing their verdict and downloading a “confidential report” of their own investigation. Help decreases from case to case, so students gain independence. The Jukumari, the bear from the Oruro Carnival, guides them with hints but never gives the answer.

Benefits

  • Skills instead of opinions: students learn to answer an environmental question with evidence: reading a trend, a p-value and its limits.
  • They learn to say “we don’t know”: for example, Cordillera Real rainfall shows no clear trend (p = 0.47), and APU doesn’t force a conclusion.
  • Self-paced and free: it runs in any browser and doesn’t depend on the teacher knowing about satellite data.

Intended impact
In the dry season, up to 27% of La Paz’s water comes from meltwater (Soruco et al., 2015). The city faced water rationing in 2016 and a red alert in August 2026. APU’s analysis of 300 months of MODIS data shows the Cordillera Real’s dry-season snow cover declining by 0.28 points per decade (p = 0.008). APU doesn’t solve the water crisis: it prepares the generation that will face it, starting with students in La Paz and El Alto. The same method already covers 11 regions, and 5 of them show a statistically real loss. The next step is a classroom pilot in La Paz schools.

Tools, languages and software

  • Frontend: JavaScript (vanilla) with Vite 5, HTML and CSS; installable for mobile use in landscape mode.
  • 3D: CesiumJS 1.122 with Cesium ion (World Terrain, Sentinel-2, Bing and Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles), and a 3D globe.
  • Live NASA services: GIBS (true-color and MODIS snow imagery), EONET (natural events) and Terra satellite tracking with satellite.js.
  • Data processing: Google Earth Engine (MODIS MOD10A1 v061 and GLIMS), NASA Giovanni (GPM IMERG V07) and GRACE/GRACE-FO (JPL RL06.1). Also NOAA’s ONI index for El Niño.
  • Statistics: Python scripts and an in-browser module for Mann-Kendall, Sen’s slope with 95% CI and the Hamed-Rao autocorrelation correction.
  • Infrastructure: Firebase (anonymous, Google and email authentication; Firestore for progress), Vercel hosting, GitHub Actions for CI and daily data backups, html2canvas for downloadable reports.
  • Design: HTML and Playwright mockups. The code is open source under the MIT license.
  • Hardware: none required beyond a computer, tablet or phone with a browser.

Creativity

  • Students produce the answer instead of receiving it: every lesson and case is built around investigating.
  • The data becomes visible: the time series plays in sync with a 3D mountain.
  • It’s rooted in Bolivian culture: the name APU and the Jukumari as guide, presented in a galaxy-themed interface.
  • It teaches scientific honesty: an inconclusive result is a valid verdict, not a failure.

Factors the team considered

  • No invented numbers: every figure comes from a real, cited source. Missing data is shown as “data coming soon”, and illustrations are labeled as such.
  • Scope honesty: MODIS measures snow cover, not water volume, and APU doesn’t use temperature because it doesn’t measure it.
  • A single learning path for everyone: the same method from start to finish, with help that fades gradually.
  • Privacy: only a nickname is stored, with no real names, ages or photos, and users can delete their account.
  • Accessibility and reliability: mobile landscape support, 44 px minimum touch targets, and fallback images and data when live services fail.
